School & learning · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

quote verb and noun

repeat someone’s words; cite

also quotation, quotations, quotes, cite, citation, as he says, as the saying goes, passage, extract (from a book), excerpt, excerpts, misquote

classical

Cic. N.D. 1.113: librōs (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Orat. 2.290: auctōrēs (Lewis & Short)

prōferō, prōferre, prōtulī, prōlātum

verb, conjugation

to bring forward, quote, cite

To bring something out before people: books, witnesses, authorities, a person’s words. Its other common senses are to carry out, to stretch out, to put off (diem prōferre) and to make known (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • ut ait (ut dīcit) — as he says (bringing in a quotation)

    phrase: put inside or after the quoted words · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 3.5: animusque aeger, ut ait Ennius, semper errat; Hor. Ep. 2.1.51: ut criticī dīcunt

    The usual way to quote in Cicero: the words run on in his sentence and ut ait names their author.

  • laudō, laudāre, laudāvī, laudātum — to cite (an author or witness as authority)

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Brut. 44: auctōrem laudāre; M-O s.v. cite (a source)

    The old sense “to name” (Gell. 2.6.16); used of the person cited, not of the words. Its everyday sense is to praise (see praise).

  • locus, locī m. — a passage (of a book), a quotation

    noun, second declension; plural locī in this sense · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 1.7: locōs quōsdam trānsferam (Lewis & Short); Traupman 30

    A passage of an author has the plural locī, places loca (Lewis & Short); hence the house’s collections of locī classicī.

  • excerptum, excerptī n. — extract, excerpt

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Quint. 2.15.24: ex Gorgiā Platōnis (Lewis & Short, s.v. excerpō); Sen. Ep. 33.3 (Lewis & Short)

    A passage picked out of a book; to make extracts is excerpere (Cic. Inv. 2.4; Plin. Ep. 3.5.10, nihil umquam lēgit quod nōn excerperet).

  • afferō, afferre, attulī, allātum — bring forward, adduce (a reason, an example)

    verb, conjugation · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 4.3.23: quam causam afferam? (Lewis & Short); Traupman 367

Examples

  • animusque aeger, ut ait Ennius, semper errat neque patī neque perpetī potest, cupere numquam dēsinit.

    and a sick mind, as Ennius says, always wanders, can neither suffer nor endure, never stops wanting.Cic. Tusc. 3.5

  • et ego cautius posthāc historiam attingam tē audiente, quem rērum Rōmānārum auctōrem laudāre possum religiōsissimum.

    and from now on I shall touch on history more carefully when you are listening, whom I can cite as the most scrupulous authority on Roman history.Cic. Brut. 44

  • aliīs verbīs pōnere

    to misquoteTraupman 346

See also phrase, author, source, praise, context.
